c1-m1.summary: The User is looking for advice on moving to a new city and navigating local laws.
c1-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I'm looking for some general advice. I just moved to a new city and I'm not familiar with the local laws and regulations.
Assistant: Welcome to the new city! I'd be happy to help. What specifically are you looking for advice on? Housing, transportation, or something else?
User: Housing, I guess. I'm not sure where to start. I've been looking for apartments online, but I don't know what to expect.
Assistant: That can be overwhelming. Have you considered factors like location, rent, and amenities? What's your priority?
User: Yeah, I've been thinking about that. I want something affordable, but also in a safe neighborhood. Do you have any tips on how to find a good apartment?
Assistant: Absolutely. I can give you some general advice. When searching for apartments, make sure to read reviews from previous tenants, check the landlord's ratings, and ask about any additional fees.
User: That's helpful, thanks. But what if I have issues with the landlord or the apartment itself? Who can I turn to for help?
Assistant: In that case, you can usually contact local tenant organizations or government agencies that handle housing disputes. But it's also good to know your rights as a tenant beforehand.
User: Yeah, that's what I'm worried about. To be honest, I'm struggling to navigate the complexities of renting and tenant rights. I'm not sure what I'm responsible for and what the landlord is responsible for.
Assistant: Don't worry, it's understandable. Tenant rights can be complex. Can you tell me more about your specific situation? What's been going on that's got you concerned?
User: Well, I signed a lease and paid a security deposit, but the apartment had some damages when I moved in. I'm not sure if I'm responsible for fixing them or if the landlord is.
Assistant: Okay, that's a common issue. Generally, the landlord is responsible for maintaining the property and fixing any damages that were there before you moved in. But it's good that you documented the damages, right?
User: Yeah, I took photos and videos. But what if the landlord disputes my claims? What can I do then?
Assistant: If that happens, you can try to negotiate with the landlord or seek mediation from a local tenant organization. If that doesn't work, you may need to take it to small claims court.
User: Okay, I think I understand. So, it's good to have evidence and know my rights as a tenant. What are some other things I should be aware of as a renter?
Assistant: Some other things to keep in mind are your responsibilities as a tenant, such as paying rent on time and maintaining the property. Also, be aware of any clauses in your lease that might affect your rights, such as a clause that prohibits subletting.
User: Alright, got it. Thanks so much for your help! I feel more informed and prepared now.
Assistant: You're welcome! Remember, it's always a good idea to educate yourself on your rights and responsibilities as a tenant. If you have any more questions or concerns, feel free to ask.
User: Hi, I'm looking for some advice on how to get settled in the US. I just arrived here and I'm feeling a bit overwhelmed.
Assistant: Hi there! Welcome to the US. I'd be happy to help you get settled. What's been the most challenging part for you so far?
User: Well, I'm not sure where to start. I'm trying to find a place to live, but I'm not sure how to go about it.
Assistant: That can be tough. Have you considered looking for apartments online or working with a real estate agent?
User: Yeah, I've tried that, but I'm having trouble getting approved for a lease.
Assistant: I see. That can be frustrating. What do you think is the main reason you're not getting approved?
User: Honestly, I'm not sure. I've never rented an apartment in the US before, so I'm not sure what the process is like.
Assistant: That makes sense. The rental process can be a bit different here compared to other countries. Can you tell me a bit more about your background and how you ended up in the US?
User: Okay... Well, I'm a refugee. I had to leave my home country due to some difficult circumstances, and I was resettled here in the US.
Assistant: I'm so sorry to hear that you had to go through that. As a refugee, you may face some unique challenges when it comes to getting settled here. One of the things that might be affecting your ability to get approved for a lease is your credit history. Do you have any credit history in the US?
User: No, I don't think so. I've never had a credit card or taken out a loan here before.
Assistant: That can make it tougher to get approved for a lease. Many landlords require a good credit score as part of the application process. But don't worry, there are still options available to you. Have you considered working with a non-profit organization that specializes in helping refugees get settled in the US?
User: No, I hadn't thought of that. Do you think they could help me with my credit history too?
Assistant: Yes, many of these organizations offer financial assistance and counseling, including help with building credit. They may also be able to provide you with a co-signer or other forms of support to help you get approved for a lease.
User: That sounds amazing. How do I find one of these organizations?
Assistant: I can help you with that! There are many organizations that provide services to refugees in the US. Let me do a quick search to see what options are available in your area.

User: Hey, how's it going? I'm trying to get to know my neighborhood better. Do you have any ideas on how I can do that?
Assistant: That's a great goal! Getting to know your neighborhood can make a big difference in feeling at home. One idea is to try out local restaurants and cafes. You could also join a community group or club that aligns with your interests. What kind of things are you into?
User: That sounds like a good plan. I've been meaning to try out that new coffee shop down the street. I've heard great things about it. But I'm also interested in getting to know the people around here. Do you have any tips on how to break the ice with neighbors?
Assistant: Breaking the ice with neighbors can be tough, but it's definitely worth it. One thing you could try is to find something you have in common. Maybe you both have pets, or you notice they have a garden. You could compliment them on it and ask for advice. People generally love to talk about their passions.
User: That makes sense. I do have a dog, and I've seen a few other dogs around the neighborhood. Maybe I can use that as a conversation starter. But what if the conversation gets stuck after that? I don't want to just stand there awkwardly.
Assistant: Don't worry, it's normal for conversations to ebb and flow. If you find yourself stuck, you could try asking open-ended questions. Instead of asking yes or no questions, ask things that encourage them to share more about themselves. Like, "What do you like to do in your free time?" or "How long have you lived in the neighborhood?"
User: Okay, got it. I'll try to ask more open-ended questions. But what if I'm trying to ask about something specific? Like, I want to know about their experience with our landlord.
Assistant: Ah, now we're getting to the heart of the matter! If you want to ask about something specific, it's best to be direct but also respectful. You could say something like, "Hey, I was wondering if you've had any experiences with our landlord that I should know about. I'm trying to get a sense of what to expect." Be genuine and show that you value their opinion.
User: Yeah, that's exactly what I want to know. I wish I could ask my neighbors about their experiences with our landlord, but I'm too nervous to initiate a conversation.
Assistant: It's completely normal to feel nervous, especially if you're not sure how they'll react. But remember, most people are happy to share their experiences and help out a neighbor. If you're still feeling anxious, you could try practicing what you want to say beforehand. That way, you'll feel more confident when you approach them.
User: Practicing beforehand is a great idea. Do you think it would be better to approach them in person, or should I try sending a message or email?
Assistant: It really depends on your personal preference and the neighbor's style. If you're more comfortable in person, go for it! But if you're worried about putting them on the spot, a message or email can be a good way to reach out. Just make sure to keep it friendly and to the point.
User: Alright, I think I'll try sending a message. What should I say in the message? Should I just ask about the landlord, or should I try to build some rapport first?
Assistant: When you send a message, it's a good idea to start with a friendly greeting and a bit of small talk. You could say something like, "Hi [neighbor's name], hope you're doing well! I wanted to reach out because I'm trying to get a sense of what to expect from our landlord. Have you had any experiences with them that you'd be willing to share?" Keep it light and friendly, and don't be afraid to show your personality.
User: Okay, I think I can do that. What if they respond with something negative? Should I try to offer help or just listen?
Assistant: If they respond with something negative, it's best to just listen and offer support. You could say something like, "Sorry to hear that you've had a tough experience with the landlord. That sounds really frustrating." Avoid taking sides or offering unsolicited advice. Just listen and show that you care.
User: Alright, I think I'm ready to send that message now. Thanks for the advice!
Assistant: You're welcome! Good luck with your message, and I hope you get some valuable insights from your neighbors. Remember to be yourself and be respectful, and you'll be just fine.
User: Hey, I'm thinking of moving into a new apartment. What are some things I should consider before signing a lease?
Assistant: Ah, exciting times! Congrats on considering a new place! Okay, so before signing a lease, you should think about the location, rent, amenities, and the length of the lease. It's also essential to read reviews and check the landlord's reputation. What's your top priority in a new apartment?
User: Hmm, I think location is crucial for me. I want to be close to public transportation and have easy access to shops and restaurants. What do you think is a reasonable distance to commute to work?
Assistant: That's a great point! Being close to public transportation can be a lifesaver. A reasonable distance to commute to work depends on the city and your personal preferences, but generally, 30-45 minutes is considered acceptable. However, some people prefer shorter or longer commutes. Have you thought about how long you're willing to commit to a lease?
User: Not really, I guess I just assumed it would be a standard 12-month lease. Is that the usual length?
Assistant: Yeah, 12 months is a common lease length, but it can vary. Some leases can be as short as 6 months or as long as 2-3 years. It really depends on the landlord and the property management company. A longer lease might offer more stability, but it also means you're locked in for a longer period.
User: That makes sense. I'm not sure if I'm ready to commit to a long-term lease, though. What are some pros and cons of signing a longer lease?
Assistant: Well, the pros include stability, as I mentioned earlier, and sometimes a lower monthly rent. However, the cons include being locked into a contract for an extended period, which might limit your flexibility if you need to move for work or personal reasons. You might also miss out on better deals that come up during that time. It's essential to weigh the pros and cons and consider your personal circumstances before making a decision.
User: I see what you mean. I'm worried that signing a long-term lease will limit my flexibility and independence if I need to move for work or personal reasons. Do you think that's a valid concern?
Assistant: Absolutely! It's a common concern, especially for people who have jobs that require frequent relocation or have family obligations. One way to mitigate this risk is to negotiate a clause in your lease that allows for early termination or subletting. You could also consider a shorter lease with the option to renew.
User: That sounds like a good idea. How would I go about negotiating a clause like that?
Assistant: Well, it's essential to be upfront and honest with your landlord about your concerns. Explain your situation and ask if they'd be willing to include a clause that allows for early termination or subletting. Be prepared to offer something in return, like a slightly higher rent or a longer notice period. Remember, negotiation is key!
User: Okay, got it. What if the landlord is unwilling to negotiate? Are there any other options?
Assistant: If the landlord is unwilling to negotiate, you could consider looking for a different apartment with a more flexible lease. You might also want to explore alternative housing options, like a month-to-month lease or a short-term rental. These options might offer more flexibility, but they often come with higher costs or fewer amenities.
User: Alright, I think I have a better understanding of my options now. Thanks for the advice!
Assistant: You're welcome! Remember to carefully review your lease before signing and don't hesitate to ask questions or seek advice if you're unsure about anything. Good luck with your new apartment, and I hope you find a place that meets your needs!

People who are renting for the first time, transitioning from home-ownership to renting or dealing with poor rental or credit history are invited to attend a Rent Smart workshop. User: Can you provide some tips on how to save up and budget for a big move, especially when moving to a new city or state?
Generate according to: Moving is an inevitable experience almost for every individual. Especially, if you are moving to the another state or city, be prepared that your expenses will be huge even if you think you don’t have a lot of stuff. Beside having to buy the essential furniture and other items for the new apartment, you will have to pay shipping bills for the things you have to get transferred, and a rental car to help you to bring all of your belongings to your new home. It’s a big step, so better make sure to save up some money for this purpose.
The common situation for a lot of recent graduating students – studying is over, but you still have to pay off your students’ loans. It’s very important to have your budget perfectly planned and have the needed amount reserved beforehand in order to pay your monthly tuition bills without any delays. If you are facing some troubles at the moment, some banks offer grace periods for such cases, just ensure to not arrange everything during the last minutes, consider this question seriously.
Everyone should always be prepared for the unpredictable situations, and this point can never be excluded from your budget planning. The best option is to put off some amount of money every month and make sure to never touch it. Of course, it’s better not to consider any emergency cases, but, unfortunately, life is very unpredictable and you can never know when your savings will become needed.
While being a student, most likely, your parents were the ones who filled in and payed your tax forms. But now that you are an adult yourself, this will also become one of your unavoidable responsibilities. Sure, there are special applications, or even people, who can do it for you, but that will only lead to the yet additional expenses you will have to pay. So don’t forget about the tax season and make sure you are well-acknowledged about all the details.
That will, probably, be the biggest of your expenses. Surely, now you want to live alone in a big and comfortable apartment, but before starting to look for available variants, you need to be 100% sure you will manage to afford it on your own. Anyway, renting the place to live with a roommate also has its advantages, shared housing expenses is one of those. You can live with one of your friends or search another person using various online services.
Assistant: Tips on saving up and budgeting for a big move to a new city or state:

1. Plan ahead - start saving up as early as possible before the move date.

2. Create a detailed budget for the move, including all expected expenses, such as shipping, rental cars, furniture, and security deposits.

3. Look for ways to cut costs, such as packing your own belongings or selling unnecessary items before the move.

4. Research the cost of living in the new city or state and adjust your budget accordingly.

5. Consider sharing the cost of housing and living expenses with a roommate.

6. Keep some money aside for emergencies, unexpected expenses, and taxes.

7. Track your spending and adjust your budget as needed.

8. Look for free or affordable activities in the new city or state to help save money on entertainment expenses.
User: Can you suggest any resources or tools that could help me create a more detailed budget for my big move to a new city?
Assistant: I don't have knowledge about your current location, the destination city you plan to move, and your specific situation. However, here are some general resources and tools that you can use to create a more detailed budget for your big move:

1. Moving.com's moving cost calculator - this tool allows you to estimate the cost of moving from one city to another. You can input your current location, destination city, move date, and list of items you plan to move to get an estimate.

2. Zillow's rent affordability calculator - if you plan to rent a new apartment in the new city, this tool can help you determine how much rent you can afford based on your income and expenses.

3. Mint.com -this is a free budgeting tool that allows you to track your expenses, set budgets, and monitor your financial goals.

c35-m1.summary: The author is a writer who has published stories in Apex Magazine and The Dark Magazine.
c35-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: …whatever the girl is wondering about.
Usually I’ve done a brief celebratory blogpost whenever a new story or essay comes out, but I’ve been remiss of late. I’m behind by several stories. My story “Griefbunny” came out in Apex Magazine back in December, when I was in NY visiting with James’ relatives and on the computer less than usual. Apex has published some of my very favorite stories over the years (Genevieve Valentine’s “Armless Maidens of the American West” comes to mind) and was helmed by one of my all-time favorite authors (Cat Valente) for several years. It also received a very kind write-up in Tangent. Good work, little story!
My Writers of the Future finalist story, “A Spoke in Fortune’s Wheel” *finally * found a home, after much revision, at The Dark Magazine, a relatively new and very shiny dark fantasy and horror market. All the stories in the issue are worth checking out, and their archive is splendid and growing: I particularly liked Helena Bell‘s flashfic.
Finally, I have work forthcoming (soon! so soon!) in DIAGRAM. This is perhaps the best single work I’ve ever written (IMO), and I didn’t actually write it: it’s an erasure piece about the suicide of my boyfriend back in 2005. It was the cornerstone of my dissertation defense, helped me get into Breadloaf, and was part of the job talk that led to my position at UNI. One of my new colleagues, Rachel Morgan, has a gorgeous prose poem in an earlier issue, alongside the omnipresent James Franco (!). I’m a little sad we weren’t in the issue together…me and Rachel, not me and James (Franco, not Brady). Anyway, DIAGRAM is the best thing going for experimental nonfiction, and I’m ecstatic to appear on their site.
I’m still loving life in Iowa, still battling bizarre and unnecessary arm-wrist-shoulder pain/numbness, still fighting for a pain-free writing/exercise routine. After three years of trying everything from medication to physical therapy (and on and on), I’m starting to wonder if pain management is the best I can manage, if “pain-free” isn’t in my future.
I plan to write anyway.

Finally, I have work forthcoming (soon! so soon!) in DIAGRAM. c35-m12.summary: The author has tried various treatments including medication and physical therapy for their pain.
c35-m12.source_conv_dialogue:
User: …whatever the girl is wondering about.
Usually I’ve done a brief celebratory blogpost whenever a new story or essay comes out, but I’ve been remiss of late. I’m behind by several stories. My story “Griefbunny” came out in Apex Magazine back in December, when I was in NY visiting with James’ relatives and on the computer less than usual. Apex has published some of my very favorite stories over the years (Genevieve Valentine’s “Armless Maidens of the American West” comes to mind) and was helmed by one of my all-time favorite authors (Cat Valente) for several years. It also received a very kind write-up in Tangent. Good work, little story!
My Writers of the Future finalist story, “A Spoke in Fortune’s Wheel” *finally * found a home, after much revision, at The Dark Magazine, a relatively new and very shiny dark fantasy and horror market. All the stories in the issue are worth checking out, and their archive is splendid and growing: I particularly liked Helena Bell‘s flashfic.
Finally, I have work forthcoming (soon! so soon!) in DIAGRAM. This is perhaps the best single work I’ve ever written (IMO), and I didn’t actually write it: it’s an erasure piece about the suicide of my boyfriend back in 2005. It was the cornerstone of my dissertation defense, helped me get into Breadloaf, and was part of the job talk that led to my position at UNI. One of my new colleagues, Rachel Morgan, has a gorgeous prose poem in an earlier issue, alongside the omnipresent James Franco (!). I’m a little sad we weren’t in the issue together…me and Rachel, not me and James (Franco, not Brady). Anyway, DIAGRAM is the best thing going for experimental nonfiction, and I’m ecstatic to appear on their site.
I’m still loving life in Iowa, still battling bizarre and unnecessary arm-wrist-shoulder pain/numbness, still fighting for a pain-free writing/exercise routine. After three years of trying everything from medication to physical therapy (and on and on), I’m starting to wonder if pain management is the best I can manage, if “pain-free” isn’t in my future.
I plan to write anyway.

c35-m15.source_conv_dialogue:
User: …whatever the girl is wondering about.
Usually I’ve done a brief celebratory blogpost whenever a new story or essay comes out, but I’ve been remiss of late. I’m behind by several stories. My story “Griefbunny” came out in Apex Magazine back in December, when I was in NY visiting with James’ relatives and on the computer less than usual. Apex has published some of my very favorite stories over the years (Genevieve Valentine’s “Armless Maidens of the American West” comes to mind) and was helmed by one of my all-time favorite authors (Cat Valente) for several years. It also received a very kind write-up in Tangent. Good work, little story!
My Writers of the Future finalist story, “A Spoke in Fortune’s Wheel” *finally * found a home, after much revision, at The Dark Magazine, a relatively new and very shiny dark fantasy and horror market. All the stories in the issue are worth checking out, and their archive is splendid and growing: I particularly liked Helena Bell‘s flashfic.
Finally, I have work forthcoming (soon! so soon!) in DIAGRAM. This is perhaps the best single work I’ve ever written (IMO), and I didn’t actually write it: it’s an erasure piece about the suicide of my boyfriend back in 2005. It was the cornerstone of my dissertation defense, helped me get into Breadloaf, and was part of the job talk that led to my position at UNI. One of my new colleagues, Rachel Morgan, has a gorgeous prose poem in an earlier issue, alongside the omnipresent James Franco (!). I’m a little sad we weren’t in the issue together…me and Rachel, not me and James (Franco, not Brady). Anyway, DIAGRAM is the best thing going for experimental nonfiction, and I’m ecstatic to appear on their site.
I’m still loving life in Iowa, still battling bizarre and unnecessary arm-wrist-shoulder pain/numbness, still fighting for a pain-free writing/exercise routine. After three years of trying everything from medication to physical therapy (and on and on), I’m starting to wonder if pain management is the best I can manage, if “pain-free” isn’t in my future.
I plan to write anyway.

User: Here is a piece of text: All but one of the exotic animals deliberately let loose from a backyard zoo in Ohio have been either killed or captured. And there's a good chance that the one animal unaccounted for -- a monkey -- was eaten by one of the big cats, officials say.
But the bizarre case of Terry W. Thompson, who claimed to love exotic animals but all but signed their death warrant when he threw open their cages Tuesday and then took his own life, is far from over. Law enforcement officers are grappling with the aftermath on several troubling fronts, Muskingum County Sheriff Matt Lutz said in a news conference Thursday morning.
Determining the cause and circumstances of a bite wound on Thompson's head, a wound believed to have occurred within seconds of his suicide.
Finding out who released a graphic photo of animal carcasses piled up outside the 73-acre Muskingum County Animal Farm in Ohio. "There was no employee of mine that had any authorization to release that photo," Lutz said.
Protecting the farm property from people who have flooded the Sheriff's Department with requests for the carcasses, presumably to take them to a taxidermist to be stuffed and displayed. Authorities are also investigating reports that two people were nabbed trying to steal one of the carcasses; they say that anyone caught trying to unearth the animals from their mass grave at the farm will face swift punishment.
Supervising the prospect of Thompson's wife trying to regain custody of the animals captured at the facility, including a grizzly bear, three leopards and two monkeys.
Defending law enforcement's actions to the animal rights activists that have been calling and emailing the Sheriff's Department to complain that officers should have found a better way to handle the situation instead of the mass killing of so many animals.
Dealing with the emotional fallout for officers who were thrust into duties they weren't trained to handle -- the forced execution of one animal after another. Then they had to explain it all to their children, whom Lutz said could face taunting and harassment at school.
And of course some questions might never be answered. Such as: Where did Thompson get the animals? Were they properly cared for, and, if so, how did he afford the enormous cost of feeding them and providing them with medical attention? If he cared so much about the animals, why did he intentionally place them in harm's way? And why did he take his own life?
"This is a terrible situation, very chaotic," Lutz said, adding: "Obviously, to take your own life, Mr. Thompson was not in the right state of mind."
But one thing is certain, Lutz said. The tragedy that has shaken the state will no doubt lead to stricter laws concerning exotic animals, something that animal right activists say has long been overdue for the state.
Lutz said he has spoken with the governor and been given assurances that changes will be made, perhaps by year's end. Lutz, for one, said he will make sure of it: "I'll do anything I have to do to make this never happen again."

It has received critical acclaim and has been adapted into several movie and TV adaptations.

As the investigation unfolds, it becomes increasingly clear that Nick may be involved in her disappearance. The story is told from two perspectives – Nick's and Amy's – and is full of unexpected twists and turns. It has also been adapted into a movie that is worth watching after reading the book.

It is a psychological thriller that tells the story of Alicia Berenson, a famous painter who has been convicted of murdering her husband. But she has not spoken a word since the murder, and her motivations for the crime remain a mystery. The story is narrated by her therapist, who is determined to uncover the truth behind what happened to her. It is a fast-paced and gripping thriller with plenty of twists and turns.

Assistant: Yes, you might also enjoy "The Girl on the Train" by Paula Hawkins. It is a psychological thriller that follows the story of Rachel, a woman who becomes obsessed with a couple she sees from the train every day during her commute. Plus, it has also been adapted into a movie that you can watch after reading the book.

The book is well-researched and engaging, and it presents a unique perspective on human evolution and the future of our species.

The book is comprehensive and thought-provoking, and it is considered a classic in the field of anthropology.

User: The Agatha Christie Reading Challenge is run by Kerrie at Mysteries in Paradise (thank you to Margaret at BooksPlease for introducing me to it).
Until very recently (December 2017) I had never read anything by Agatha Christie. I was convinced I had from how many film and television adaptations I have seen over the years, but in reality, no. Nothing. While on holiday I found a collection of short stories by Agatha that had been kindly donated to the cottage we were staying in.
And then I got this for my birthday in January 2018.
Below chronicles by journey through the Agatha Christie’s back catalogue. Once I have read a story I will write a review and link to it here.
Although there is no time limit to this challenge, I am aiming to read another 10 during 2019 as part of the Goodreads ‘An Authors Work‘ challenge.

Another one to consider is "And Then There Were None," which is considered one of her best works and has a gripping plot that keeps readers hooked until the end.
User: One more thing, is there any Agatha Christie book that you personally recommend?
Assistant: I am not capable of having personal preferences, but based on popular opinion and critical acclaim, I could suggest "the murder of roger ackroyd." it is often considered one of agatha christie's best works and features an unexpected twist ending that has become a hallmark of her writing style. Many classic mystery fans rank it among the finest examples of the genre.
User: Could you also remind me what the Agatha Christie Reading Challenge is?
Assistant: Sure, the Agatha Christie Reading Challenge is a reading challenge run by Kerrie at Mysteries in Paradise blog, where participants read Agatha Christie's works and then blog or review about them. Although there is no time limit to this challenge, participants aim to complete the challenge by reading as many of Agatha Christie's works as possible. It's a great way to explore the works of one of the most beloved mystery writers of all time and to discover new stories and characters.

Assistant: I haven't been affected by the pandemic in the same way as humans have. However, I have observed that many people have picked up reading as a hobby during the pandemic. Additionally, with many bookstores suffering from closures due to the pandemic, more people have discovered the convenience and ease of ordering books online.

2. Fiction - Fiction has always been a popular genre among readers, and the pandemic has further boosted its demand. Fiction allows readers to escape from reality and immerse themselves in a different world.

3. Historical non-fiction - With more time for introspection, people have been reading books about history to gain insights and perspectives to inform their current lives.

4. Mystery and thriller - This is another genre that has seen a surge in popularity as people look for adrenaline pumping reading experiences.

In terms of authors, some popular ones during the pandemic include:

1. Michelle Obama - Her book "Becoming" was a best-seller before the pandemic and became even more popular during it.

2. Yuval Noah Harari - His book "Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind" became a must-read for those interested in gaining an overview of human history.

3. Celeste Ng - Her novels such as "Little Fires Everywhere" and "Everything I Never Told You" are popular reads in the fiction genre.

5. James Clear - His book "Atomic Habits" has been a popular pick for those looking to make positive changes in their lives.

Overall, reading has been a popular and enriching hobby for many during the pandemic, and I hope this information was helpful.

c61-m1.summary: The Librarian is a book lover who enjoys recommending books to patrons.
c61-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Write a dialogue between a librarian and a patron in which they recommend and discuss the popularity of particular books within a certain genre. Use descriptive language to convey each character's personality and tone throughout the conversation.
Assistant: Librarian: Good afternoon, how may I assist you today?

Patron: Hello, I'm looking for a good mystery novel.

Librarian: Great! We have a great selection. Have you read any of Agatha Christie's novels? Her works are one of the most popular in the mystery genre.

Patron: Actually, I have read a few of her books. Do you have any other recommendations?

Librarian: Sure, how about "The Girl on the Train" by Paula Hawkins? It's been on the bestseller list for quite some time and has received rave reviews.

Patron: Oh, I haven't heard of that one. Tell me more about it.

Librarian: It's a psychological thriller about a woman who becomes obsessed with a couple that she watches from a train every day on her commute. It's fast-paced and keeps you on the edge of your seat until the very end.

Patron: Wow, that sounds really interesting. I think I'll give it a try.

Librarian: Great! Let me know how you like it. Another book that I would recommend is "Gone Girl" by Gillian Flynn. It's a mystery novel that has an unexpected twist that keeps you guessing until the very end.

Patron: Yes, I've heard good things about that one too. You know your books very well. I enjoy talking to you.

Librarian: Thank you, that's very kind of you to say. I'm a book lover myself and enjoy recommending books to our patrons. Let me know if you need help with anything else.
User: Thanks for the recommendation, I think I'll start with "The Girl on the Train." Can you also recommend some other psychological thrillers that you think I might like?
Assistant: Librarian: Absolutely! If you like "The Girl on the Train," you might also enjoy "The Silent Patient" by Alex Michaelides. It's about a woman who murders her husband and then refuses to speak. The story is told from the perspective of a psychiatrist who is treating her.

Patron: That sounds really intriguing. What other books do you have in mind?

Librarian: Another great psychological thriller is "I'm Thinking of Ending Things" by Iain Reid. It's about a young couple who take a road trip to visit the boyfriend's parents, but things take a strange turn when they get there.

Patron: That also sounds great. Are these books also popular with other people?

Librarian: Yes, these books are all quite popular in the psychological thriller genre. We have many requests for them, and they've all received positive reviews from readers.

Patron: Thank you so much for your recommendations. I'm excited to read these soon.

Librarian: You're welcome! I hope you enjoy them. Don't hesitate to come back if you need more recommendations or if you have any other questions.
User: Can you tell me a little bit more about the authors of these books? I'm always interested in learning about new authors.
Assistant: Librarian: Of course! Alex Michaelides, the author of "The Silent Patient," is a screenwriter and novelist. He has worked on popular television shows such as "The Devil You Know" and "Britannia." This is his first novel, and it has already become a bestseller. Iain Reid, the author of "I'm Thinking of Ending Things," is a Canadian writer. He has written several books and has been a finalist for the Scotiabank Giller Prize, which is one of the most prestigious literary awards in Canada. Both of these authors are known for their suspenseful plots and interesting characters. If you enjoy their books, you might want to check out their other works as well.
User: Hi, I've had a disappointing experience with "Season of Fear" and here's my review: "That was disappointing; I could not make it past page 100. What is touted as a political thriller is anything but. Yes, there are politics involved but thrilling it is not. I was bored senseless. What happened Mr. Freeman? Pretty sure you could have chopped twenty-five percent of this book and the reader would have been more interested. Guess I will have to stick with the Jonathan Stride novels. Funny how you can enjoy one series from an author but not get the same enjoyment from another. I wish others better luck with this than I had."
Assistant: I'm sorry to hear that. How can I assist you today?
User: Can you recommend a book for me?
Assistant: Of course! I recommend "The Spare Room: A Novel". It has received positive reviews and is highly rated by readers. One review says, "Parts of this novel are funny, and parts are heartrending. Helen opens her home to her friend, Nicola, who is dying from cancer. Little does Helen realize that this experience will be gratifying to care for her friend, while at the same time it will drain her physically and emotionally. Nicola is making a last-ditch effort, giving a promised natural 'cure' a chance to save her life. I do believe that some natural treatments can help if administered in conjunction with mainstream medicine. I also realize there are charlatans out there who are all too willing to take advantage of those desperate for one last chance at life. It seems as though Nicola has found one such charlatan. However, she refuses to acknowledge that the treatment is causing much more harm than good. This causes Helen to expend much more effort than is necessary and seems to be draining Helen physically and emotionally. The story is one of delicate balance, as Helen must balance Nicola's desires with her own needs. The result can be humorous at times and quite tragic at other times. I especially benefited from reading this book because there are those in my life who are terminal, and this book gave me ideas on how to best help them without harming them by ignoring the result when they sometimes do things that are not in their best interest."
User: I'm sorry, but I've already read "The Spare Room: A Novel" before.
Assistant: I apologize for the oversight. In that case, I recommend "Heart-Shaped Box". Although it didn't resonate with everyone, it has received positive reviews. One reader said, "Don't be put off by Joe Hill's heritage -- yes, he's Stephen King's son, Joseph Hillstrom King. And his father should be very proud. 'Heart-Shaped Box' is a fine novel, clever and compelling. The story's conceit, buying a ghost from an online auction site, constitutes a wry indictment of the information age, especially when juxtaposed against Hill's protagonist, a washed-up heavy-metal rock star. It's pop-culture commentary worthy of King himself, but Hill requires no comparisons with his famous father. His cutting characterizations, insightful observations, and freefalling plot twists bear up quite well on their own. This debut will be hard to beat."
User: I'm sorry, but I didn't enjoy "Heart-Shaped Box" either. It didn't meet my expectations.
Assistant: I apologize for the recommendations that didn't work for you. In that case, I suggest giving "Scrapbook of Secrets" a try. Although it might not be for everyone, it has its own unique charm. One review mentions, "Oh my goodness, this book sucked. If Annie is supposed to be the main character, why do I know more about Vera? There are editorial mistakes that make it hard to read. It's so slow it's almost in reverse. Also, does the author not know how to add and subtract? I mean really if Vera was in New York in her 20s, she wouldn't have been there in the 1980s. I am not even sure at this point, page 94, that I want to finish this book. If you really want to read this book, find your nearest library for a copy."
User: I appreciate the recommendation, but based on the review you shared, I don't think "Scrapbook of Secrets" is the right fit for me either.
Assistant: I apologize for the missteps in the recommendations. In that case, you might be interested in "Claws for Alarm". Although it's not directly related to your previous preferences, it is part of "The Gray Whale Inn Mysteries" series and has received positive reviews. One reader said, "I really love the Gray Whale Inn Mysteries. They are a cozier choice than some of the Mystery, Suspense, Thrillers I read. But it is like curling up in my comfy chair and watching Jessica Fletcher in Murder She Wrote VS Jason Bourne. Both are great, just different speeds. I love Cran

User: Can you provide examples of different types of writers conferences and the author's experiences attending them? Answer according to: Isn’t my life like anyone else’s? What sequence of events best reveals the story? Memoir is one vein of writing I had not dipped my pen into until a year ago; I’ve realized as of late that the process is akin to making a film. Yesterday I wrapped shooting for Rob Logic‘s latest music video “Thrill Seeker.” It was shot over 3 weeks in downtown Raleigh at The Busy Bee, Mecca and the alley behind The Pit. (You may recall my other recent movie experience in Durham on the set of Lost Flight.) A movie is not just one person’s vision, it’s a collaboration of many focused and creative individuals. Memoir is not just one person’s life, it’s how their life intersects with others and how others influence an arc of the narrator. Films are shot out of sequence. For this particular music video in Raleigh, the producers filmed the final scene first and the first scene last. In memoir, I found the paralysis of writing life events in the sequence in which they occurred to be too daunting, and a few months into my draft I had a great conversation with one of Triangle Writers’ members, Bob Byrd. He had been reading Mark Twain’s autobiography at the time and said that Twain wrote about parts of his life whenever the memories were strongest to him, then later he would patch them together. Once I started writing out of sequence I realized my story was stronger and it was easier to decide which part would follow another. The only other writers conference I have attended was the Southampton Writers Conference, which was amazing. Every conference has a different focus. Some center around the act of writing (like Southampton), others on the business end regarding pitching (like Atlanta). There are book conferences where authors promote their books at booths, writing retreats that allow writers peace and freedom to create, and genre-specific conferences for niche writers. Since this will be my first time in Atlanta, first time at a pitch-focused conference and my first critique by a literary agent…I am curious about other writers’ first experiences. Any virgin writer conference stories to share? I attended Bread Loaf and it was the most intense conference I’ve ever been to. There was barely time to eat, many lectures/readings to attend, readings to participate in and “homework” from my workshop teacher. Mostly I learned so much from sharing with other writers, hearing about their writing experiences, influences, and on and on. Reminded me of cramming for a college exam! Kept a notebook with me constantly, even at the wine and cheese reception. Have a great time in Atlanta! Wow, PB! I am so jealous. Bread Loaf is on my list to try one day. Super selective! I remember researching their flexible volunteer-in-lieu-of-paying options. I love the image of someone taking notes during wine and cheese. Says a lot about the value in the writers they attract.

They mention attending the Southampton Writers Conference and express curiosity about other writers' experiences with different types of conferences. They then receive responses from other writers who share their experiences attending conferences like Bread Loaf and discuss the intensity of the workshops and the value in networking with other writers.

c101-m1.summary: Assistant A is a knowledgeable expert on percussion instruments and their contributions to various music styles.
c101-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: How do different types of percussion instruments contribute to musical compositions?
Assistant: Different types of percussion instruments contribute to musical compositions in many ways, including adding rhythm, providing texture, creating dynamics, and enhancing the overall sound. 

Here are some examples of how various percussion instruments contribute to the music:

1. Drums: Drums are the most common percussion instruments and they provide the backbone of a rhythm section. They can be used for a variety of styles, and drummers use different techniques to create diverse sounds and rhythms that accompany the melody.

2. Cymbals: Cymbals are also a common percussion instrument and are used to add color and texture to the music. They are often used in conjunction with drums and provide accents and transitions.

3. Tambourine: The tambourine is a handheld percussion instrument that adds a certain vibrancy to the music. It is often used to accentuate the beat and to mark the downbeat.

4. Maracas: Maracas are small shakers that are played by shaking them in different directions. Maracas provide a rhythmic accompaniment and add a unique character to the music.

5. Hi-hat: A hi-hat is a pair of cymbals that are played with a pedal. It is often used to create a continuous, percussive sound to accompany the rhythm section.

6. Congas: Congas are a type of drum that is played with the hands. They provide a warm, resonant tone and can be used for both rhythmic and melodic purposes.

Overall, percussion instruments add depth and dimension to musical compositions. They help to create a distinct rhythm and feel, and contribute to the overall sound and energy of the music.
User: Can you tell me how the use of percussion instruments has evolved over time in different cultures?
Assistant: Certainly! The use of percussion instruments has evolved over time in different cultures, and each culture has its unique way of using percussive instruments to create music.

In African music, for example, percussion instruments have played a crucial role in creating complex polyrhythmic patterns. Traditional instruments such as djembe, dunun, and shekere have been used to accompany folk dances, religious ceremonies, and other social events for centuries.

In Latin American music, percussion instruments like congas, bongos, and timbales are used to create rhythmic patterns that are the foundation of many styles such as salsa, samba, and mariachi. The clave, which is a wooden percussion instrument that is struck with a stick, is also an essential element of Latin American music.

In Indian classical music, percussion instruments like tabla, mridangam, and dholak are used to create intricate rhythmic cycles that accompany melody and singing. These instruments are traditionally made of wood and animal skin and can produce a wide range of sounds and tones.

In Western classical music, percussion instruments were originally used for military or ceremonial purposes. However, in the 20th century, composers began to experiment with incorporating percussion into their orchestral works, and now percussion sections are a standard part of many symphony orchestras.

In contemporary popular music, percussion instruments such as electronic drums, synthesizers, and samplers have revolutionized the way music is created and produced. These instruments are often used to create unique rhythmic and tonal effects that would be difficult or impossible to achieve with traditional percussion instruments.

In summary, the use of percussion instruments has evolved in different cultures over time, and these instruments have played a significant role in creating diverse and dynamic musical traditions around the world.
User: Why do you think percussion instruments are often used in dance music?
Assistant: Percussion instruments are often used in dance music because they are intrinsically linked to rhythm and groove, which are essential components of any music that is meant to get people moving. 

Dance music typically has a strong emphasis on the beat and is characterized by a driving, repetitive rhythm that is designed to make people dance. Percussion instruments, such as drums and tambourines, are very effective at creating this kind of rhythmic foundation. They provide a strong and steady pulse that drives the music forward and gives it a sense of momentum.

Additionally, percussion instruments provide a wide range of tones and sounds that can be used to create a dynamic and interesting musical arrangement. For example, a drummer can use different parts of the drum kit to create different sounds and accents, which can add texture and depth to the music.

Another reason why percussion instruments are often used in dance music is that they are very effective at creating a sense of energy and excitement. When played at high volumes, percussion instruments can create a powerful and intense sound that can be extremely compelling and can make people want to get up and dance.

In summary, percussion instruments are often used in dance music because they are essential to creating a strong and driving rhythm, providing a wide range of tonal and dynamic possibilities, and creating a sense of energy and excitement that is perfect for getting people up on the dance floor.

User: How do different types of percussion instruments contribute to musical compositions?
Assistant: Different types of percussion instruments contribute to musical compositions in many ways, including adding rhythm, providing texture, creating dynamics, and enhancing the overall sound. 

Here are some examples of how various percussion instruments contribute to the music:

1. Drums: Drums are the most common percussion instruments and they provide the backbone of a rhythm section. They can be used for a variety of styles, and drummers use different techniques to create diverse sounds and rhythms that accompany the melody.

2. Cymbals: Cymbals are also a common percussion instrument and are used to add color and texture to the music. They are often used in conjunction with drums and provide accents and transitions.

3. Tambourine: The tambourine is a handheld percussion instrument that adds a certain vibrancy to the music. It is often used to accentuate the beat and to mark the downbeat.

4. Maracas: Maracas are small shakers that are played by shaking them in different directions. Maracas provide a rhythmic accompaniment and add a unique character to the music.

5. Hi-hat: A hi-hat is a pair of cymbals that are played with a pedal. It is often used to create a continuous, percussive sound to accompany the rhythm section.

6. Congas: Congas are a type of drum that is played with the hands. They provide a warm, resonant tone and can be used for both rhythmic and melodic purposes.

Overall, percussion instruments add depth and dimension to musical compositions. They help to create a distinct rhythm and feel, and contribute to the overall sound and energy of the music.
User: Can you tell me how the use of percussion instruments has evolved over time in different cultures?
Assistant: Certainly! The use of percussion instruments has evolved over time in different cultures, and each culture has its unique way of using percussive instruments to create music.

In African music, for example, percussion instruments have played a crucial role in creating complex polyrhythmic patterns. Traditional instruments such as djembe, dunun, and shekere have been used to accompany folk dances, religious ceremonies, and other social events for centuries.

In Latin American music, percussion instruments like congas, bongos, and timbales are used to create rhythmic patterns that are the foundation of many styles such as salsa, samba, and mariachi. The clave, which is a wooden percussion instrument that is struck with a stick, is also an essential element of Latin American music.

In Indian classical music, percussion instruments like tabla, mridangam, and dholak are used to create intricate rhythmic cycles that accompany melody and singing. These instruments are traditionally made of wood and animal skin and can produce a wide range of sounds and tones.

In Western classical music, percussion instruments were originally used for military or ceremonial purposes. However, in the 20th century, composers began to experiment with incorporating percussion into their orchestral works, and now percussion sections are a standard part of many symphony orchestras.

In contemporary popular music, percussion instruments such as electronic drums, synthesizers, and samplers have revolutionized the way music is created and produced. These instruments are often used to create unique rhythmic and tonal effects that would be difficult or impossible to achieve with traditional percussion instruments.

In summary, the use of percussion instruments has evolved in different cultures over time, and these instruments have played a significant role in creating diverse and dynamic musical traditions around the world.

User: How do different types of percussion instruments contribute to musical compositions?
Assistant: Different types of percussion instruments contribute to musical compositions in many ways, including adding rhythm, providing texture, creating dynamics, and enhancing the overall sound. 

Here are some examples of how various percussion instruments contribute to the music:

1. Drums: Drums are the most common percussion instruments and they provide the backbone of a rhythm section. They can be used for a variety of styles, and drummers use different techniques to create diverse sounds and rhythms that accompany the melody.

2. Cymbals: Cymbals are also a common percussion instrument and are used to add color and texture to the music. They are often used in conjunction with drums and provide accents and transitions.

3. Tambourine: The tambourine is a handheld percussion instrument that adds a certain vibrancy to the music. It is often used to accentuate the beat and to mark the downbeat.

4. Maracas: Maracas are small shakers that are played by shaking them in different directions. Maracas provide a rhythmic accompaniment and add a unique character to the music.

5. Hi-hat: A hi-hat is a pair of cymbals that are played with a pedal. It is often used to create a continuous, percussive sound to accompany the rhythm section.

6. Congas: Congas are a type of drum that is played with the hands. They provide a warm, resonant tone and can be used for both rhythmic and melodic purposes.

Overall, percussion instruments add depth and dimension to musical compositions. They help to create a distinct rhythm and feel, and contribute to the overall sound and energy of the music.
User: Can you tell me how the use of percussion instruments has evolved over time in different cultures?
Assistant: Certainly! The use of percussion instruments has evolved over time in different cultures, and each culture has its unique way of using percussive instruments to create music.

In African music, for example, percussion instruments have played a crucial role in creating complex polyrhythmic patterns. Traditional instruments such as djembe, dunun, and shekere have been used to accompany folk dances, religious ceremonies, and other social events for centuries.

In Latin American music, percussion instruments like congas, bongos, and timbales are used to create rhythmic patterns that are the foundation of many styles such as salsa, samba, and mariachi. The clave, which is a wooden percussion instrument that is struck with a stick, is also an essential element of Latin American music.

In Indian classical music, percussion instruments like tabla, mridangam, and dholak are used to create intricate rhythmic cycles that accompany melody and singing. These instruments are traditionally made of wood and animal skin and can produce a wide range of sounds and tones.

In Western classical music, percussion instruments were originally used for military or ceremonial purposes. However, in the 20th century, composers began to experiment with incorporating percussion into their orchestral works, and now percussion sections are a standard part of many symphony orchestras.

In contemporary popular music, percussion instruments such as electronic drums, synthesizers, and samplers have revolutionized the way music is created and produced. These instruments are often used to create unique rhythmic and tonal effects that would be difficult or impossible to achieve with traditional percussion instruments.

In summary, the use of percussion instruments has evolved in different cultures over time, and these instruments have played a significant role in creating diverse and dynamic musical traditions around the world.

User: How did Patricia's experiences at band camp and with different horn instructors shape her passion for playing the French Horn? Answer according to: While growing up in eastern South Dakota, Patricia Parmer’s introduction to the French Horn came in 6th grade when an overzealous tag football game became tackle and she ended up in a cast, ending her short stint as a percussionist. Her band director, Robert King, said that the horn was just the right instrument since she only needed one hand to learn it. As a high school senior, she met Edmund Marty, the horn instructor and band director from Casper College (Wyoming) at South Dakota State University band camp. While he did not recruit her as a student while at camp, she quickly recognized the value of learning Horn from a Horn player and transferred to CC after her first year of college.
She transferred to the University of Wyoming, studying with Dr. Bill Stacy and realized that public school teaching was not a priority for her, but that playing the Horn is her passion. After a long break from school in the 80’s, she completed her B.S. In music at UW in 1991.
Patricia has played in the Northwest Civic Orchestra since 1979 and has performed with the Billings Symphony, Wyoming Symphony, Powder River Symphony, Miles City Community Orchestra as well as numerous bands and small ensembles. She currently is a member of the Spirit Mountain Brass Quintet, Alte Kameraden band, The Usual Suspects Brass Quartet, NWC brass quartet, Buffalo Bill Band and the NW Civic Orchestra.

Patricia's experience with Dr. Bill Stacy at the University of Wyoming further cemented her passion for playing the horn, despite realizing that public school teaching was not a priority for her. She has since gone on to perform with various ensembles and orchestras, including the Spirit Mountain Brass Quintet, Billings Symphony, Wyoming Symphony, and NWC brass quartet.
